text: Thank you, Mr. Speaker. Ten years ago today. June 4, 2014, in Moncton. I think everybody in this Chamber remembers where they were that night and the days that followed. We lost three RCMP officers — Constable Doug Larche, Constable Dave Ross, and Constable Fabrice Gevaudan. Constable Darlene Goguen and Constable Eric Dubois were there too, and their courage that day is part of the same story. These were people who put the uniform on and went toward it, which is what they do every day of the year, most days without any of us noticing. Ten years on, the loss is still felt by those families, by the city of Moncton, by this province and by this country. Mr. Speaker, the least we can do is keep supporting the men and women who serve in law enforcement, and keep working at the kind of communities where this does not happen again. I would ask members to hold those officers and their families in their thoughts today. We will remember them. Thank you, Mr. Speaker.
strategy: short declarative sentences, plain memorial cadence, first-person recollection

text: Thank you, Madam Speaker. Good news out of Albert County this week. Jennifer Shelby, of Hopewell Hill, is now a published contributor to the Journal of L.M. Montgomery Studies — her essay is titled "Of Daydreams and Influence". It came out as part of the "Writers and Artists Respond" celebration for Montgomery's 150th birthday. Madam Speaker, I did not know before this that there was a whole journal devoted to L.M. Montgomery studies, and I suspect I am not alone in that, but there is, and one of my constituents is in it. The essay is a reflection on Montgomery's influence on Jennifer's writing and on her life as an Atlantic Canadian woman. Imagination, resilience — those are the themes she takes up, and she does it in a way that is very personal and, I would say, poetic. It speaks to the literary talent we have in that part of the province and to how much Montgomery's legacy still means. Congratulations to Jennifer Shelby. May her words keep inspiring readers across the country.
strategy: opens on the county and the journal, dry humour, tighter rhythm

text: Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I want to mark the day. Ten years ago, June 4, 2014, in Moncton, three RCMP officers were killed in the line of duty. Constable Doug Larche. Constable Dave Ross. Constable Fabrice Gevaudan. Two others, Constable Darlene Goguen and Constable Eric Dubois, were wounded, and I do not want them left out of what we say here. Mr. Speaker, officers go out on an ordinary shift and take on a risk the rest of us do not, and most days it ends fine and nobody thinks about it. That day it did not. The families are still carrying it. So is that city, and so is this province and this country. What we owe them, I think, is to keep backing the people who serve in law enforcement and to keep at the work of building communities where this kind of violence does not happen again. Their memory should push us in that direction. We will remember them. Thank you, Mr. Speaker.
strategy: Speaker addresses the Chamber directly with a personal aside and a request to reflect

text: Thank you, Mr. Speaker. Ten years on. June 4, 2014, in Moncton — I do not need to say much more than the date for members to know what I am talking about. Constable Doug Larche, Constable Dave Ross and Constable Fabrice Gevaudan were killed that day doing their job. Constable Darlene Goguen and Constable Eric Dubois were there and were shot as well, and their names belong in this too. Mr. Speaker, that is the risk that comes with the uniform, every day, whether anything happens or not. The families live with what happened. Moncton lives with it. This province and this country do too. All I would say is this: keep supporting the men and women in law enforcement, and keep doing the work that makes communities where a day like that does not come around again. I would ask members to think about those officers and their families today. We will always remember them. Thank you, Mr. Speaker.
strategy: Understated, conversational, low-ceremony; hesitation and a moment-of-silence idiom

text: Thank you, Madam Speaker. I'd like to welcome members of the New Brunswick Psychiatric Association, who are with us in the gallery today — and I believe some of them are up there right now. Among our guests are members of the association's Board of Directors. These are dedicated professionals, and the work they do is essential to New Brunswickers' mental health and well-being. The association keeps working closely with the Department of Health, and that collaboration is helping strengthen our system of care. I'll have more to say on that a little later today. Thank you. Thank you, Madam Speaker.
strategy: warm spoken welcome with gallery gesture, contractions, slightly loose ordering

text: Thank you, Mr. Speaker. Ten years today. The fourth of June, 2014, in Moncton. I do not think I have to describe that night to anybody in this Chamber. Constable Doug Larche. Constable Dave Ross. Constable Fabrice Gevaudan. Three RCMP officers killed doing their job, and Constable Darlene Goguen and Constable Eric Dubois were there that night as well, and I want their names said too. What that day put in front of all of us, Mr. Speaker, is the risk these officers carry on an ordinary shift. Most days nothing happens and none of us give it a thought. That day something did. The families are still living with it. So is Moncton, so is this province, so is the country. What I would ask of members is that we keep backing the men and women who serve in law enforcement, and that we keep doing the work on the kind of communities where a day like that does not happen. Their memory ought to push us toward that. We will always remember them. Thank you, Mr. Speaker.
strategy: Personal recollection, names front-loaded, short clipped sentences
